text:
Alfred North Whitehead was born in Ramsgate, Kent, England, in 1861. He was educated at Sherborne and subsequently studied mathematics at Trinity College, Cambridge, earning his B.A. in 1884, where he graduated as fourth wrangler. He taught mathematics and physics at Cambridge until 1910, during which time he co-wrote *Principia Mathematica* with Bertrand Russell, a work considered a major contribution to mathematical logic of the 20th century.
Later, Whitehead moved to London and then to the United States in 1924, joining the faculty at Harvard University as a professor of philosophy. His philosophical work, including *The Concept of Nature* (1920) and *Process and Reality* (1929), challenged prevailing scientific materialism by advocating for an event-based or "process" ontology, where fundamental reality is composed of interrelated occasions of experience. His philosophy, known as "process philosophy," posited that relations are primary, and he viewed God not as a ruler but as a receptive entity completed by the world's activity, inspiring process theology.
